Homelab · Backup · Proxmox

Backup the 3-2-1 way and the restore test: a backup only counts once it has been restored

Most backup stories end at the same point: the backup ran – but nobody ever tested whether it can be restored. Here is how I back up my Proxmox host and how I test the restore without endangering anything running.

Serge Zabolotny · 2026-10-27

  • Backup
  • 3-2-1-Regel
  • Proxmox
  • vzdump
  • Restore-Test
  • Homelab
  • Uptime Kuma

The 3-2-1 rule in one sentence

Three copies of the data (the original plus two backups), on two different storage media, with one in a different location. A second disk in the same machine protects against a disk failure, but not against theft, fire or a power surge – which is exactly the gap the last number closes. How the series covers this is in access and backups in the home server.

My baseline: vzdump with a retention rule

On the Proxmox host with the split LXC containers, a backup runs daily to a separate disk, keeping seven daily, four weekly and three monthly copies:

vzdump <CTID> --storage <backup-storage> --mode snapshot \
  --prune-backups keep-daily=7,keep-weekly=4,keep-monthly=3

In addition, Uptime Kuma reports when a service goes down. That does not replace a restore test, but it quickly shows when something is wrong. I secure access to the host as described in zero trust for the homelab.

The restore test in four steps

Safety rule: always restore to a new, unused container ID, never to the ID of a running container. And remove the test container’s network before starting it so it cannot clash with the original.

  1. Pick a backup: list the archives in the backup storage and choose a recent one.
  2. Restore to a new ID: pct restore 999 <archive> --storage <target-storage>
  3. Remove network, start, check: pct set 999 -delete net0, then pct start 999. Does the service run? Is the data complete and recent?
  4. Clean up and note it down: pct stop 999 && pct destroy 999. Record the date, archive and result – that is your evidence.

For virtual machines the command is qmrestore; the principle stays the same. Repeat the test at fixed intervals, say once a quarter, and after every major change to the setup.

Why this matters professionally too

Backup and recovery are among the measures customers may ask service providers about under NIS2. A documented restore test is concrete evidence. For me it is also one of the things that should be a given in every project, from MeisterMeld to the server environment.

Checklist

  • Daily backup to a separate disk, with a retention rule
  • At least one copy in a different location
  • Restore test on a new ID, result documented
  • Monitoring with notifications (e.g. Uptime Kuma)
